scenario.name: NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer
scenario.overview: Imagine a hardware wholesaler whose tiny brass screws are packed automatically inside millions of furniture kits across the world. Attackers steal the wholesaler warehouse login because no second-factor pocket code was required, slip an automatic spring-loaded trap inside the screw box lid so every carpenter who opens the box unknowingly fetches a lockpicking kit, and silently launches a credential thief using a trusted built-in workshop tool. In this scenario (T1195.001, NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: maintainer Account Takeover, then automatic preinstall Execution, then silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Maintainer Account Takeover, then Automatic preinstall Execution, then Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Maintainer Account Takeover & Malicious preinstall Hook Publish
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1195.001 - Compromise Software Dependencies)
stages.description: Breaking into a busy component-maker shipping account that lacked a second pocket-code lock, the intruder releases a tiny routine-looking version bump containing a spring-loaded lid script designed to snap open the instant any workshop unpacks the crate. By compromising maintainer npm credentials that did not enforce two-factor authentication (2FA) for package publishing, the threat actor pushed trojanized versions (ua-parser-js@0.7.29, coa@2.0.3, rc@1.2.9) containing a "preinstall": "node preinstall.js" hook in package.json (an npm lifecycle hook that executes arbitrary shell commands on the host machine automatically before the package is even imported by any application code). Because many upstream libraries declare loose semver ranges (such as ^0.7.0 or ^2.0.0), any developer or CI job running npm install without a strict lockfile automatically pulled the newly published malicious version. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Maintainer Account Takeover & Malicious preinstall Hook Publish / ⇠#1 ALERT T1195.001) from Node ① (#1 Hijacked NPM Account & Payload Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens).

stages.title: Stage 2: Automatic preinstall Execution & curl Download of sdd.dll
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059.007 - JavaScript / T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell)
stages.description: The moment a developer runs a routine morning toolbox refresh, the spring-loaded lid checks whether the workshop runs Windows or Linux, triggers a hidden helper script, and reaches outside the building to download a concealed espionage module straight into the local parts bin. When npm install ran on a developer workstation, node.exe executed preinstall.js, which fingerprinted the host OS (process.platform) and on Windows spawned cmd.exe /c compile.bat to invoke curl (downloading both an XMRig miner jsextension.exe from 159.148.186.228 and a malicious DLL sdd.dll from citationsheriff.com, saving the DLL locally as create.dll). On Linux workstations and CI containers, the script instead executed preinstall.sh to download and run an ELF cryptominer binary (jsextension). In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc), NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the cmd.exe /c compile.bat request succeeded on NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution & DanaBot Credential Theft). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ cmd.exe /c compile.bat / ⇠#2 ACK 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens).

stages.title: Stage 3: Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution & DanaBot Credential Theft
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion & Credential Access (T1218.010 - Regsvr32 / T1555)
stages.description: Rather than running an unfamiliar executable that guards would immediately question, the helper script hands the stolen espionage module to the workshop own official parts-registration machine set on mute, silently awakening a password thief that sweeps browser vaults and developer keys. The batch file executed regsvr32.exe -s create.dll (abusing the signed Microsoft COM registration utility with the -s silent flag to invoke the DLL’s DllRegisterServer export without displaying error popups), launching the DanaBot information stealer in memory to harvest saved Chrome/Edge browser passwords, session cookies, Windows DPAPI secrets, SSH private keys, and cloud CLI credentials. Because developers frequently hold privileged AWS, GitHub, and production SSH credentials on their laptops, CISA warned that any workstation that installed these versions had to be treated as fully compromised. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) to Developer Workstation (npm install), Developer Workstation (npm install) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the regsvr32.exe -s create.dll request succeeded on Developer Workstation (npm install) and completing the final execution objective of NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ regsvr32.exe -s create.dll / ⇠#3 ACK 1) from Node ③ (#3 NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc)) to Node ④ (#4 Developer Workstation (npm install)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens).

keySpecs.value: Block regsvr32.exe from loading unsigned DLLs located in user-writable project directories or node_modules folders via WDAC/AppLocker rules.
